newsitem.title: USA: Arguments in landmark muni tax case begin shortly.
newsitem.headline: Arguments in landmark muni tax case begin shortly.

text.p: A federal appeals court in California is scheduled to hear oral arguments on Tuesday morning in a landmark case challenging IRS' right to tax bondholders on interest earnings on troubled bond deals.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit sitting in Pasadena is set to hear Harbor Bancorp v Commissioner of Internal Revenue, a case dating back to 1992 when IRS declared as taxable $30 million in bonds sold by Riverside County, Calif., Housing Authority to build two multifamily housing projects.
One of the projects, Whitewater Garden, was never built, and the other, called Ironwood, was constructed, but not with bond proceeds.
Both deals were rushed to market on December 31, 1985, by New York City underwriter Matthews & Wright to beat a new federal curb on "arbitrage" profits that was to take effect Jan. 1, 1986.

The Securities and Exchange Commission later revoked Matthews & Wright's broker-dealer license and took other enforcement action after concluding that the Dec. 31 bond closings were "shams" because no cash actually changed hands.
The Internal Revenue Service then moved to collect nearly $68,000 in back taxes on the interest investors earned from the two bond deals.
But bondholders' attorneys argued before the U.S. Tax Court that their clients should not be punished because they and the housing authorities were unaware of wrongdoing.

The tax court rejected the argument, saying that the hastily drawn papers used at the so-called closing in late 1985 should have tipped off municipalities. And even if there were no clues, IRS does not have to take into account whether a municipality knew abaout a possible violation, tax court judges said.

Municipalities appealed the ruling. Mary Reichert, a partner with Bryan Cave in St. Louis, who is representing bondholders, said the case is critical because it is the first time IRS' commissioner has attempted to tax bondholders.
Reichert is expected to argue that bondholders, who were victims of the theft, should not be held accountable for the perpetrators of the theft.
